title: Many vs All and the Fear of God
english: A sound, not the apostles and the others. Again, if they say, 'By Beelzebul, the ruler of demons, he casts out demons' (Matt 12:24), they are not friends, they are not virtuous men. 'And my neighbors very much.' The Jews were his neighbors, if the Savior is the one speaking; and the hypocrites of virtue are significant.

They are my neighbors, and they have their own buildings near my house; for the house of the righteous is the upright conduct. For the 146th [Psalm] having heard the words of Jesus and having converted them into works, builds a house upon the rock, whereas the one building upon the sand [is foolish]. Since both have become hearers of the words of Jesus, they seem to be neighbors, they seem to be similar.

'The houses of the lawless shall undergo cleansing, but the houses of the righteous are received.' The law-breakers are not lawless, but they have the same law, yet they transgress it. But when it is said, 'Blessed are those to whom the lawless deeds have been forgiven,' those have no experience of law. 'Law-breaking brings a man to reproach'; for in a way the lawless do not even stand up for judgment so that they might be reproached. To be reproached is a lesser punishment. Therefore, those having received the law and having transgressed, these stand up 'for reproach and eternal shame.'

And that this is so, we will understand from the prophecy of Daniel; for in it this lies: 'And from the sleeping ones of the earth's dust'—he did not say 'all'—'these stand up for life, and those for reproach and for shame' (Dan 12:2). The resurrection is also found in the 91st Psalm; the ungodly stand up not to be judged. The law-breakers, those having received the law and having transgressed, the sinners, stand up for judgment. The righteous are raised up not to be judged, but to receive the promises.

Now therefore he says: 'And many of those sleeping'; for he does not count thus the ungodly who are not raised for judgment, but those standing up 'for reproach and eternal shame.' These are the sinners. The righteous [stand up] 'for eternal life.' Concerning these two ranks, the Savior also says in the Gospel: 'Those who have done the good shall come forth for a resurrection of life, but those who have done the evil for a resurrection of judgment' (John 5:29). He does not even mention the ungodly here. Since, therefore, the rank of the ungodly is set apart...

He did not say that 'all' rise up, but 'many of those sleeping'. If anyone considers this interpretation to be violent and says that the ungodly and the impious are also arranged among the 'many', we hear 'many' thus instead of 'all'; for all are many, and it is not a contradiction. However, let the 'many' be said here instead of 'all'.

And the apostle writes this: 'just as through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous, so also through the disobedience of one man many will be made sinners' (Rom 5:19). And here 'all' are signified by the 'many': all those who disobey, all those who obey. It is not a contradiction. If some are 'all', it is not necessarily that the 'many' are 'all', for example: 'many will say to my soul' or 'and fear to my known ones'. I have become a fear to my known ones, bearing this state which many reproach. Indeed, even the apostles, having been afraid, were scandalized at a certain time.

But here he speaks of a fear which is passive, which is followed by cowardice if it is not itself cowardice. It is possible also to receive a divine fear. Those observing me, knowing the mystery of my visitation and for whose sake I was crucified, had a fear equal to reverence, concerning which it is said: 'the fear of the Lord surpassed all things'; see, for what does it say: 'my known ones'.

The diligent are known by God; for the Lord knew those who were His, and they know Him. For the apostle says also to the Galatians: 'but once they did not know God, but now they know God, and even more so they are known by God' (Gal 4:9). When we know God, He knows us; for 'if anyone' 'is ignorant, he is unknown', clearly meaning that if anyone knows, he is known. Therefore, 'fear' 'to my known ones'.

Those worthy of being known, and knowing me, had a fear equal to reverence, concerning which it is said: 'then you will understand the fear of the Lord', after many mistakes. 'Those observing me fled from me'.

The Savior and Lord of us is both God and man at once. But He is seen and observed according to being man; for He is invisible being the 'image' 'of the invisible God'. And it is necessary for the image of the invisible to be invisible. But if it is said: 'he who has seen me', let 'having seen' be taken homonymously instead of 'he who observes me intelligently, he who sees me divinely, he who sees as...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Encirclement of Jesus
english: Imposing [the mystery] upon the invisible, he who also understands the mystery of the presence and the passion. Therefore, those outside are looking at me as outside, those who know Christ only according to the flesh, and such people are those about whom Paul writes: 'For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified' (1 Cor 2:2). They are of the outside and run outside, such as those are who hear in parables; for it is not the parable spoken unclearly that has made them outside, but their own external intellect has led them outside to this.

He became as if dead from the heart. The one understanding Jesus as being life—for he says: 'I am the life' (John 14:6)—and living, is the son of a living Father; for he says 'I live' because of the Father—they never forget him; for being present in their intellect, he always enlightens them, so that each one says: 'But Christ lives in me' (Gal 2:20). Such a person is in Christ and has Christ in himself, living and working. But when someone perceives him not as living nor working, he forgets him as if dead; for Christ does not live in all, but in those working according to him. And those who consider themselves to be Christians, but do not work according to Christ, do not have him living in them.

See: the foolish man lives according to wickedness, being 'more a lover of pleasure than a lover of God' (2 Tim 2:22), doing all things hedonistically. He considers the righteous man to be dead, because he is stripped of his own foolish life and does not receive it in his intellect. 'I became as a lost vessel' (2 Tim 2:21). I have not become a lost vessel, but like the lost vessel. And take for me the example: the other men being crucified beside the Savior seem to have become useless vessels, vessels of destruction. This one saying these things as if he has become the lost vessel, but not lost. Just as sin became not the same thing to others as being sin, but so that they might become the righteousness of God in him, he was made like sin (2 Cor 5:21), he was made like the lost vessel. For that men are called vessels is not unknown, and these indeed are for honor, but those for dishonor. This vessel according to Jesus is not of destruction; for he did not know sin. But it has become like the lost vessel. It has become a curse, so that it might bring blessing. But no curse brings blessing, but rather it diminishes the blessing; not—
For he was a blessed man, though cursed. This one, having become a curse, has become a cause of blessing, and not for one man, but for all who believe.

I heard the slandering of many dwelling around. I heard many slandering me, not having set themselves apart at all. The Israelites were dwelling around Jesus. They slandered him: 'He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons' (Matt 12:24). 'He is a sinner because he does not keep the Sabbath' (Matt 12:2). They were around. If those saying these things were Gentiles, they would not have been his circle. These have become a circle. For he says: 'And they encircled me like bees, Lord' (Ps 118:148). They encircled me aggressively.

In the gathering of them all at once against me. He mentioned enemies, neighbors greatly reviling him; he mentioned those attacking him from the heart; he says those dwelling around and slandering. These were gathered together at once 'to take his soul,' especially when 'nations and peoples raged and labored in vain' (Ps 2:2); for here also nations having raged were not yet entirely set apart from him or separated. 'Why did they rage?' They attacked the Hebrews more arrogantly. And the Hebrews in vain and emptily labored over the prophecies concerning me. All the things said: the hosts 'were gathered together at once, they deliberated to take my soul.' The magnitude of the attack is shown, that 'at once all were gathered together to take his soul.' Not one, nor two, nor ten, nor a thousand, but all at once. The unshakeable and the irresistible, or the not being overturned, of the soul of Jesus is signified. They hardly gathered at once to take my soul or deliberated, and they did not seize it. 'No one takes my soul from me; I lay it down from myself, so that I may take it again' (John 10:18).

They deliberated to take my soul. They have gone as far as deliberating to kill him. If he himself does not give himself, they were not able to do this. For they came greedily to seize him, he says: 'Whom are you seeking?' (John 18:3) and he says: 'Jesus the Nazarene' (John 18:5). 'I am,' as he said, 'they went backward and fell to the ground' (John 18:6). And again a second time: 'Whom are you seeking?' and he said the same to them, and they fell to the ground again. He says a third time: 'I am,' therefore me...
